title: ‘September 5’ Director Tim Fehlbaum Working on a ‘Historical Film’ Set in Berlin as Swiss Filmmakers Take on Challenges and Opportunities of Shooting in English
description: Some of the main breakouts of Swiss cinema in 2026—and the few years that precede it—share one striking commonality: they are either entirely in Eng
body:
Some of the main breakouts of Swiss cinema in 2026—and the few years that precede it—share one striking commonality: they are either entirely in English or feature large chunks of English. Think Petra Volpe’s Locarno-winning “Frank & Louis,” Damien Hauser’s festival darling “Memory of Princess Mumbi,” Denis Rabaglia’s buzzy “Butterfly Stroke” and, of course, Tim Fehlbaum’s lauded historical thriller “September 5.” 
	

	On the date that names his award-winning film, Fehlbaum joined “Quiet Land” director Ursula Meier and “Erosion” helmer Michael Koch at the Venice Production Bridge – where Switzerland is a country of focus – to discuss this very phenomenon in a panel titled: Beyond Borders: English as the New Language in Swiss Cinema? Moderated by Variety Italy and Middle East Correspondent/Rome Bureau Chief Nick Vivarelli, the discussion honed in on the benefits and challenges of shooting in English in Switzerland today. 


	Fehlbaum revealed that his next project will take place in Berlin and be shot in both German and English. “It’s set in Germany, and it’s historical, but it also has an American perspective on it. It’s always a question of how much will be in German and how much will be in English. By changing one character to a person who doesn’t understand German, you suddenly have much more English, and it’s much easier to finance.”


	Meier relayed her current experience producing “Quiet Land,” which is part of this year’s Venice Gap-Financing Market. The English-language film will star Bill Murray and Léa Seydoux, with a story set in Montana but shot in Alberta. The director is currently in pre-production, with plans to shoot next year. “For me, it’s interesting for my work to tell a bigger story, and everything in the U.S. is bigger,” she said when asked about the reasons for shooting in English.
	

	“It was a great challenge for me,” added the writer-director of penning the script. “My English is not so good, and I had a year to work on [it]. We wrote the script in French, and then it was translated. We followed [the translation process] [very closely.]” 

	The director added how much she “loves U.S. actors,” recalling working with Gillian Anderson on her Oscar-shortlisted “Sisters.” “It was so great to work with her,” she said. “I like how [American actors] embody characters. It’s very physical.” 

	Koch recently had the experience of working with a major American actor himself, having just shot “Erosion” with lead Peter Sarsgaard. The drama will reunite the director with the non-professional actors of “A Piece of Sky” for a film observing the dynamics between a foreigner and the local Swiss farmers in a small mountain village. It was Fehlbaum who made the bridge between Koch and Sarsgaard, following their collaboration in “September 5.”

	“For me, this choice to shoot with an English-speaking actor was, from the beginning, a creative choice,” emphasized the director. “It was, in a sense, the concept of the film, also. Unlike my previous film, which was shot with only non-professionals and chose a very specific mountain world from the inside, I wanted this time to turn it around and look with the eyes of a stranger to this world. It was clear from the beginning that it had to be the eyes of a foreigner. The second thing that intrigued me a lot was to put a famous actor like Peter together with nonprofessional actors from the Swiss mountains, which sounds like a really weird combination, but it was something I wanted to explore.”

	The filmmaker interjected to say he does not believe English to be the new language of Swiss cinema, but that it is certainly “a part of it.” Working in a different language was a “very interesting experience” for Koch, who noted how, when verbal communication is limited, other creative forms of interaction arise. “This was the interesting thing to observe: how people from different worlds come together and share something beyond verbal communication.”



	

					“Frank & Louis,” courtesy of Sundance Film Festival
	



	Having a major American actor as the lead also changed the financing process for Koch, who picked up on Vivarelli’s metaphor to say it felt like the film “felt more like a Ferrari” financing-wise. “It’s a bit more [money] you have to get, but it’s also easier. It went quite fast, I have to say. It was also possible because [Sarsgaard] really wanted to [make the film], otherwise, we couldn’t afford it.”
	

	Fehlbaum made a key point when looking back at his experience of shooting several films in English: “It has to come from the story.” He recalled being told by producers he needed to make his feature debut, “Hell,” in English, as it was a post-apocalyptic sci-fi. “It was before Netflix, and people told me I couldn’t get it financed.” The director felt the choice didn’t make sense for the film, and trusted his gut. The results proved his choice correct, with the film doing very well domestically and internationally. 

	For his follow-up, “The Colony,” Fehlbaum decided to shoot in English despite the script not quite calling for it. The lukewarm response to the film confirmed the director’s thesis that it only makes sense to make a film in English if the choice also makes sense diegetically. That was a very clear call with “September 5,” which was told from the point of view of American broadcasters in Munich during a hostage crisis in the 1972 Olympics.

	The director also highlighted how English offers a much wider vocabulary to writers, especially those who are German-speaking. “The English language, compared to German, [has] three times as many words,” he said. “In scriptwriting, you always want [scripts] to be short. In English, it’s cool that you can use just one word when in German you’d have to write a whole sentence. For subtext, English is better. In German, [words are] very specific.”

	But Fehlbaum warns writers and directors of the dangers of rushing to technology, especially AI, to take on the task of translating. Recalling a meeting with a translator who told him AI is taking on their positions on jobs such as translating scripts and dialogue on set, the director emphasized how great an experience he had with a seasoned linguist on “September 5.” “We first wrote [the script] in German and it was clear that we would get a translator on board. He not only translated [the script] but had a different perspective and made it much more American. It’s important to get authenticity.” 

	As for the challenges, all three directors brought up the difficulties of having to communicate in their second language with actors when under the overbearing pressures of being on set. “I realized the language barrier is much bigger than I would’ve thought,” said Fehlbaum. But Koch offered a positive counterpoint: “There’s also a nice thing about that. Because then [actors] are really challenged to think about: what does he mean? So they start to participate in this process also.”
	

	And there’s also the fact that Switzerland is a country already built on the idea of multiple languages, with German, French, Italian, and Romansh as the nation’s official languages. In that context, all three filmmakers agreed that, while English films are on the rise, the idiom is just another card on their table—and Swiss directors are eager to play their hands.

title: ‘Possible Love’ Review: Korean Master Lee Chang-dong Returns With a Beautifully Mature, Quietly Colossal Relationship Drama

body:
One of the key moments from Lee Chang-dong‘s last film, 2018’s “Burning,” still glows bright in the memory. A girl mimes eating a tangerine, and explains the knack for making it convincing: don’t try to pretend there is a tangerine, try to forget there is not. It’s a little zen koan that rhymes imperfectly in “Possible Love,” Lee’s wonderfully rich and deep new movie, when Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon, delivering one of the most intricate performances of the year) is entranced by the fancy house by the sea to which she has been invited. “It’s like a place from a novel!” she exclaims, only for her husband to scoff gently at the idea that Mi-ok reads novels at all. “Ok then,” she says agreeably, refusing to be any less enthused, “It’s like a place from a novel I haven’t read.” 
	

	Absences so clearly delineated they read as presences; dreams so unattainable the yearning for them takes on mass and dimension, maybe even brick-and-mortar form. “Possible Love” is not a mystery, but it is rife with such little mysteries. And yet Lee’s elegantly unshowy filmmaking, typified by DP Kim Ji-yong’s coolly discreet photography, and the inner life that Jeon suggests is being lived behind Mi-ok’s bright, disingenuous eyes, are grounded in the prosaic reality, trenchantly observed, of Korean classism and labor exploitation. It is perhaps only Lee Chang-dong who can so seamlessly integrate such radically separate themes and moods, with every event being of consequence but nothing feeling forced. “Possible Love,” ostensibly a relationship drama tracking two marriages from opposite sides of the social divide, unfolds with surprise and inevitability held in such perfect balance that each moment feels like it’s telling you something you’ve always known, but have just never thought of before.
	

	Mi-ok is married to Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu, from Lee’s “Peppermint Candy” and “Oasis”) a heavy-industry worker who has recently been fired following an unsuccessful strike at the factory that is the area’s biggest employer. Their son Cheol (Jung Seop) seems to have inherited his father’s taciturn disposition. He’s a quiet, watchful boy with the habit of hiding in closets or lurking near doorways the better to hear how adults talk when they think no kids are around. But perhaps his father is not naturally so surly; later will come a moment when Ho-seok’s dam breaks and we realize, with a stab of profoundest sympathy, just what a vast reservoir of hurt it has been holding in check.

	There has been a rash of suicides following the factory-wide layoffs. At a funeral for one fallen friend Ho-seok, feeling shunned by his erstwhile strike comrades, gets into a soju-fuelled altercation. It’s defused by Mi-ok, but they’ve caught the eye of Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong, of “Parasite” fame), a pretty, well-heeled aspiring filmmaker shooting footage for a high-minded documentary about the human cost of corporate downsizing. Ho-seok declines to participate, but Mi-ok becomes Ye-ji’s interview subject, and then, after a fashion, her friend. There is perhaps a subtle critique here, of the predatory instincts of the filmmaker towards their subject, of the desire to invade someone else’s life and shape their reality according to your own will. These are instincts that Lee has somehow been born without; his subjects may be fictional creations but, especially as embodied by such a fine cast, they’re allowed to live and breathe their own private existences, their own personal idiosyncrasies, yielding characters who are almost as unknowably strange as, in your secret heart, you know yourself to be.

	Their unequal friendship does however bring Mi-ok into the social orbit of Ye-ji’s moneyed, attractive husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). She is a little awed by him at first, made almost shy in his presence  — he’s the kind of enigma who is solid only when viewed in your peripheral vision, as though his surface dazzle makes him hard look at directly. For his part, Sang-woo is supportive, in a casual and vaguely patronizing way, of his wife’s filmmaking ambitions, and politely tolerates these less fortunates, until his offhand attention is piqued by Mi-ok’s tipsily flirtatious fascination with him. At dinners together, and then at the wealthy couple’s fabulous seaside property, complete with winding forest path, private beach and a guard hut manned by Min-sik (Kang Chang-gwon), Sang-woo’s childhood playmate-turned-deferential factotum, uneasy alliances, easily ruptured, interconnect the foursome. Little Cheol looks on, unnoticed, from the back of every room.
	

	“Possible Love” carries the brief dedication “In memory of Dekalog 10 by Krzysztof Kieślowski and Krzysztof Piesiewicz,” and after Asghar Farhadi’s “Parallel Tales” is the second in a planned 10-film, multi-auteur project remaking Kiezlowski’s masterpiece. Lee’s film is wholly original, and has no relation to the storyline of “Dekalog 10,” which is inspired by the Tenth Commandment: “Thou shalt not covet.” And yet his movie is mischievously multi-layered enough that the idea of covetousness does open up heady new seams of interpretation. For one thing covetousness, as opposed to the more concrete sins like theft or murder or adultery, is a thought crime, and almost all that goes on here, happens within the minds of the characters (again, what kind of wizard can make such interiorized action so endlessly compelling?) 

	For another, you only covet what you do not have, but you have to be aware you do not have it. Mi-ok is houseproud about her small family home, and the never-used marble picnic table that Ho-seok, in happier times, built with the idea it would be a gathering point for chatty groups of friends to share a drink. But returning home after some time with Ye-ji and Sang-woo, their place suddenly looks shabby and cheap. Another time, Mi-ok remembers a childhood incident when her mother, who washed cars for a living, slapped the hose out of her hands when she caught Mi-ok imitating her. The adult Mi-ok understands that her mother was scared by the idea that her daughter might have the same life she did. But when we teach our children to dream big, and to want bigger lives than we had, are we helping them or, given the array of social forces that will in all likelihood deny them any mobility, are we simply setting them up for a discontented adulthood? When Mi-ok sees Cheol bonding with the groundskeeper and hosing the villa’s manicured garden, she turns away and lets him continue to water the plants.

	As written in the Bible, the Tenth Commandment is a stern prohibition. In “Dekalog 10”, it became a drolly comic cautionary tale. But in “Possible Love” it could almost be a statement of reward. Behave without hypocrisy and without cruelty and you open yourself up to betrayal and exploitation, but you may also earn the gift of not-coveting, of understanding you have no need to envy or aspire to the trappings of someone else’s life. 
	

	Mi-ok and Ho-seok share a calm, lovely moment on their brand new marble bench. They have found that there can be some comfort in being on the righteous side of a struggle even, perhaps especially, if it is lost. There can be comfort in discovering that the pages of the book never read were blank all along. There can be comfort in knowing that what you have may be paltry, but it is better than cherishing the illusory outline of something you do not have at all. This shimmering, sonorous work, from one of our greatest living directors, moves through the peculiar landscapes of human interaction with certainty, eccentricity and grace to remind us that, no matter how good the pretence, there is no tangerine.

schema.headline: ‘Possible Love’ Review: Korean Master Lee Chang-dong Returns With a Beautifully Mature, Quietly Colossal Relationship Drama

title: ‘Woman Unknown’ Director May el-Toukhy Talks the Torment of World War II ‘Horizontal Collaborators’ and Venice’s Female Director Snub: ‘It’s a Structural Problem’

body:
In “Woman Unknown,” May el-Toukhy takes a closer look at women accused of having relationships with German soldiers during World War II.

	“When we started to build a story about a ‘horizontal collaborator,’ we realized that, during and after the war, the female body became part of national identity. But in Denmark, it wasn’t really explored.” 

	Initially, she wanted to make a film about the witch hunts after the Reformation in the 1500s. 
	

	“It was difficult to relate to the perpetrators because many of them were just maniac. And I’m interested in ambiguity,” she says. Then, she came across an old newspaper photo of a woman with a swastika painted on her back.


	“You can find very similar stories that are thousands of years old. The shaving of a woman’s hair or her public shaming for ‘sharing’ her body is a very old concept. Even today, it’s still happening in many armed conflicts.”

	Still, this suffering tends to be ignored by historians. The title of her film references that silence as well.

	“I was inspired by Belarusian writer Svetlana Alexievich who wrote ‘The Unwomanly Face of War.’ She gathered these testimonies from women who talked about having their periods in war zones, hiding in sheds, and giving birth. It’s rare to have such recollections of the female experience during or after the war,” says el-Toukhy.

	For Marie, a housemaid and a nanny, the future looks bright: she’s about to marry her wealthy employer. But in the weeks leading up to liberation in 1945, she must do her best to survive and ensure that her secrets don’t catch up with her. 
	

	“Our main character wants to remain unknown, but we haven’t told stories about these women either. When you see their photographs in the archives, they’re often labeled ‘unknown woman.’ Also because people didn’t care.”

	Ironically enough, “Women Unknown” has already made headlines because of Venice’s decision to include only one female director in the main competition. The festival later added documentary “Naza,” co-directed by Rachel Szor.

	“Obviously, I’m delighted to have been invited to this historic festival. But I would have loved to be in the company of more female directors in the competition. I do believe it’s a structural problem,” notes el-Toukhy.

	“We discussed how the idea of publicly shaming women is an old concept. Not having enough films by women is also an issue that goes way back. It’s reflected in the budgets we work with and the talent that wants to be involved. Even journalists talk about male directors differently than they talk about women. I’ve never heard a female director called a ‘genius’ – and I read many articles about male geniuses.”

	What’s the solution? 

	“Everyone has to chip in and be a part of it. I will now have a chance to discuss this issue through my film, which is rather aptly called ‘Woman Unknown’. I’m happy to do so, even though the circumstances surrounding me being in the main competition are what they are.” 

	“We have a lot of work to do in order to change that.”

	May el-Toukhy is interested in new solutions. As previously announced by Variety, she’s also part of the new Dogma 25 movement. You can find the full manifesto here.

	“It’s always healthy to disrupt your process as a filmmaker,” she says.

	“Dogma 25 is very much about how we make films. Even though I heard many yeses while making this film, I still feel like I had to run much faster. That that kind of sprint doesn’t necessarily benefit the result.”

	She adds: “The way we have to work is almost unbearable. You finish a film and you’re completely stressed out and exhausted. I could make another big European arthouse drama in the future – I’m not saying goodbye to that format. I just think we really need to rethink the way we make movies.”
	

	As in her previous films, el-Toukhy doesn’t care much for typically likable protagonists. In “Queen of Hearts,” she followed a woman who seduced her teenage stepson. In “Woman Unknown,” Marie makes questionable choices as her carefully built facade threatens to collapse.

	“It would be a betrayal to my sisters around the world if I only portrayed women as saints. It’s important that we tell stories about complex women in a nuanced way, just as we do with male characters. That rings truer to life.” 

	She wanted to stick to a female perspective throughout the story.

	“Early on, we made a rule that we would never reproduce the male experience of war. [Marie] goes out of the house, but the streets represent danger. People are celebrating and there’s euphoria, chaos and vigilantisms. Her safe space is at home, but then insecurity and danger move in. Suddenly, there’s no safe space anymore.”

	For the longest time, no one dared to criticize “the liberators” and their brutal methods. 

	“It would have been harder to tell this story 25 years ago when those generations were still alive. Some audience members will still be shocked or angry because their grandfather was part of the resistance movement, which became very strong in Denmark right up to the liberation. But not everyone should have been a part of it.” 

	“It’s important to have discussions about what actually happened so that we don’t recreate false narratives. It’s hard to change the direction you’re going in if you’re not looking back.”

title: Susan Sarandon Says She’s ‘Still Had Movies Taken Away Recently’ Over Palestine Support: ‘There Are Agencies That Are Telling People Not to Hire Me’
description:
Susan Sarandon said she’s “still had movies taken away recently” over her outspoken support of Palestine. 

	At the Venice Film Festival press confe
body:
Susan Sarandon said she’s “still had movies taken away recently” over her outspoken support of Palestine. 

	At the Venice Film Festival press conference for her new film “The Echo Chamber” on Sunday, Sarandon was asked if she thinks the narrative is changing in Hollywood when it comes to the conflict in Gaza. In 2023, the Oscar winner was dropped by her agency UTA after comments she made at a pro-Palestinian rally and said earlier this year she felt she was shunned by the industry for calling for a ceasefire in Gaza.
	

	“I think that the narrative has completely changed in terms of historical relevance of Palestine and the ties of Zionists with America and our politics. That has been a major revelation for people. How much money the United States gives to Israel, nobody really understood that,” Sarandon began.


	“I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still,” she continued. “But that’s the power structure. I think within the people, certainly internationally, I feel welcome.” 

	“The Echo Chamber” hails from Italian director Andrea Pallaoro and filmed in Italy and Belgium. Sarandon stars in the romantic drama, which was Bernardo Bertolucci’s final screenplay, alongside Luca Marinelli and Alicia Vikander. 

	Sarandon said that Pallaoro was told not to work with her but did so anyway. “I thank Andrea for that, because he doesn’t listen to the warnings,” she said. 

	“There has been a change in terms of the general public, but there are still positions in my industry that are held by Zionists who have not relaxed their feelings towards me,” Sarandon concluded. “But I found my family, I found my people and I’m OK.”

schema.headline: Susan Sarandon Says She’s ‘Still Had Movies Taken Away Recently’ Over Palestine Support: ‘There Are Agencies That Are Telling People Not to Hire Me’

title: Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’
description: Roma filmmaker Alina Șerban broke barriers long before she set foot on the red carpet this week at the Venice Film Festival, where her feature-lengt
body:
Roma filmmaker Alina Șerban broke barriers long before she set foot on the red carpet this week at the Venice Film Festival, where her feature-length directorial debut, “I Matter,” world premieres in the Venice Spotlight section.

	Rising from an impoverished background to become a celebrated stage star in Romania, the actress and directing debutante has defied all odds to reach the starry heights of the Lido. Billed as the first feature from a female Roma director to screen at an A-list festival, “I Matter” marks the latest chapter in her life-long quest to reframe the narrative around her marginalized community. 
	

	Șerban, however, is taking it all in stride.


	“I’m nervous about the pressure of being ‘the first’ — all the firsts,” she tells Variety. “But I also have this immense relief, and the feeling of being grateful that I managed to pull through something almost impossible.”

	Inspired by Șerban’s own life, “I Matter” tells the story of a young Roma woman studying to be an actor. She’s faced with the threat of being kicked out of her orphanage and must suddenly embrace her identity and confront the reality of making it through life on her own. Based on the 2021 short of the same name, whose festival run included New Directors/New Films, it’s produced by microFILM, 2Pilots Filmproduction, Frakas Prods. and Lemming Film, with international sales handled by Pluto Film.

	For Șerban, the premiere is a capstone in what has already been a remarkable career. Raised in poverty in Bucharest, she was placed in a state-run orphanage at an early age before becoming the first member of her family to graduate from high school. After attending Bucharest’s Academy of Theatrical Arts and Cinematography, she was accepted into NYU’s Tisch School of the Arts, then later earned a master’s degree from the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London.
	

	When she returned to Romania, she mounted an acclaimed one-woman show about her life, focusing not only on the rampant discrimination she faced, but on her triumphs and joys. By her 30th birthday, Șerban had written and staged pioneering plays that championed a radical, feminist, Roma perspective — trying, she says, “to show the humanity of these people. Not to portray them as victims nor villains. Not to self-exoticize. But also to celebrate ourselves.”

	“I Matter” stars newcomer Denisa Farcaș, bringing both vulnerability and determination to a lead role that she invests with her own life experience, according to the director. Șerban describes working with Farcaș and her co-stars as a “collaborative process,” one in which the group delved deep into “what it means to be accepted” as Roma women while giving the young actors space to “express themselves — to feel that they also own the story.”

	This isn’t Șerban’s first visit to the Venice Film Festival; she attended in 2023 with the cast and crew of Goran Stolevski’s “Housekeeping for Beginners,” in which she had a supporting role. But this year’s experience will be something else entirely for the director. Nearly two dozen of the cast members of “I Matter” will be in attendance — including the 16 child performers who populated the film’s orphanage — while Roma band Mahala Rai Banda will serenade the red-carpet arrivals.

	“This is such a historical moment for me, and also for the Roma community,” Șerban says. “It’s a moment of celebration. And I want to look back and say I did everything in my power for the people in the team to [share this] moment. And also to put into the world a message of dignity, of celebration, of pain that needs to be seen.”

schema.headline: Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’

title: Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers’ Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: ‘We Are the Opposite of Politicians … We Are the Antidote’
description: Wim Wenders has clarified his much-discussed statement about filmmakers’ role in politics that kicked off a firestorm at Berlin Film Festival earlie
body:
Wim Wenders has clarified his much-discussed statement about filmmakers’ role in politics that kicked off a firestorm at Berlin Film Festival earlier this year.

	Wenders was at the center of a heated debate at the Berlinale in February after the celebrated German filmmaker, who served as jury president, said during the opening press conference that filmmakers “should stay out of politics.” 


	“We have to stay out of politics because if we make movies that are dedicatedly political, we enter the field of politics,” Wenders said at the time. “But we are the counterweight of politics, we are the opposite of politics. We have to do the work of people, not the work of politicians.”
	

	The statement then dominated the discourse at the festival, with nearly every filmmaker and actor facing a question about politics — including the ongoing conflict in Gaza and ICE raids in the U.S. — during their respective press conferences. Author Arundhati Roy even pulled out of the festival in protest, and festival director Tricia Tuttle had to put out a statement in response to the frenzy.

	Asked to reflect on his statement Sunday during a press conference at Venice Film Festival, where he is presenting his latest documentary “From Inside Out — The Architecture of Peter Zumthor,” Wenders said that he “could repeat the same thing,” though admitted he “could be more explicit.”

	“What I said then was, as filmmakers, we are the opposite of politicians. We have empathy. Politics work without empathy; that’s all I said,” Wenders, who sported an “Imagine Peace” shirt, began. “We have a very different thing. I’m not working with a mindset of politicians, we are working with a mindset of empathetic people. And we are into changing things, politics are into confirming what is.”
	

	He continued, “That’s what I said and was quoted as ‘We have to stay out of politics,’ and that is not what I said, because it’s not what I said now and I said the same thing then. The frame of filmmakers is a different mindset than the mindset of politicians, and we should not work with that mindset. We work with a different set of rules. I said it again, and I hope you’re not misquoting me and say we have to stay out of politics, because we do the opposite. We are the antidote.”

	At Venice’s opening press conference earlier in the festival, jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal weighed in on the topic, saying that movies are “fundamentally, undeniably political.”

	“Look, we could say, how are we possibly here talking about movies right now when the world is in a state of emergency?” she said. “To me, the answer has something to do with empathy. I think that film allows an opening into an opportunity to find empathy inside of ourselves.”

schema.headline: Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers’ Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: ‘We Are the Opposite of Politicians … We Are the Antidote’

title: ‘From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor’ Review: Wim Wenders’ Latest 3D Documentary Is an Architectural Marvel
description: The screen is usually a canvas, but it becomes a window to an enormous room in Wim Wenders’ latest 3D documentary, “From Inside Out – The Architectu
body:
The screen is usually a canvas, but it becomes a window to an enormous room in Wim Wenders’ latest 3D documentary, “From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor.” Within that room unfolds the tale of the Swiss architect of the title, told in occasionally laborious ways. It spends much of its two-hour runtime teaching you how to watch it, and like your average high school class, you might not see the value of its instruction until it eventually comes in handy. In that vein, Wenders presents some magnificent things in the film’s final third, sensations which emerge like Zumthor’s own views on the function of his buildings, which he ties to human experience, understood by its inhabitants gradually, and then all at once — from the inside out.
	

	Beginning with shots of concave corners and convex, monolithic surfaces, “From Inside Out” engenders curiosity before taking academic detours. These come courtesy of Zumthor himself, whom we first meet as a ghostly projection upon sleek, minimalist surfaces, emanating from the 1980s. Like the Holocaust survivors whose poetry populated the walls in Wenders’ “Anselm” — his 3D retrospective on the works of sculptor Anselm Kiefer — Zumthor’s words become inseparable from each room the camera explores, and each building the architect believes ought to feel at one with its surroundings.


	We eventually meet Zumthor in the present: an unassuming man in his eighties, whose descriptions of form, function and fluidity often repeat themselves, but whose sincerity and wisdom are hard to shake. As the film explores houses, museums and other Zumthor commissions, the architect’s use of light and natural materials becomes as important as the theoretical people he intends to fill each space — or, in the case of complicated restorations, the people who inhabited them decades ago. Wenders depicts these ghosts of past and future through dramatizations of curious travelers, whose whispering voiceover offers scattered thoughts on where they stand.
	

	There’s a tinge of humor, too, in Zumthor’s stubbornness when designing someone’s home, as the conceptual clashes with the preferential. However, the architect eventually gives way to use and function first, despite valuing the aesthetics at hand (not to mention, his collaborations with local artisans). It isn’t long before Wenders introduces the idea that Zumthor’s spaces are only as important as what goes inside them, when he first contrasts old and contemporary footage of museums he designed, each filled with deeply personal art installations — some of them about war.

	Zumthor himself doesn’t have the most interesting personal history — at least, not as far as this film is concerned — so Wenders’ exploration can come off as superficial at first. However, this ends up part and parcel of the structure. It echoes the feeling of approaching a marvelous building from afar, and entering its sterile lobby, before slowly discovering its mischievous secrets.

	Although some scenes and enactments can meander, they give way to a moving triptych of projects whose presentation feels, in a way, climactic. One is a home deeply personal to Zumthor. Another is a Nordic installation built in tribute to women killed in witch trials, which feels terrifying to walk through — a kind of infinitude accentuated by Franz Lustig’s 3D cinematography. And the third is arguably Zumthor’s magnum opus: his sprawling, amoebic construction housing the permanent collection at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, whose planning and completion the doc depicts in detail.

	By the time the building is finished (and visited by a number of filmmakers, including Ava DuVernay and Werner Herzog), Wenders’ camera moves in tandem with Zumthor’s own abstract notions of the art pieces needing to feel horizontally equal, with none being granted more or less importance than any other. The sprawling gallery seems to have no beginning or end. Its bends extend endlessly, revealing pockets and side rooms with rough, exposed concrete contrasting the gilded grandeur of the pieces on display.

	It takes a while to realize this, or at least to internalize it, but the film’s own architecture is not dissimilar, with what feels like winding segues that add up to an experience of fluid expanse, of great wandering, and ultimately, of soulful appreciation. Certainly, no one is beholden to a film this demanding, but Wenders wields his 3D camera to craft a perfect marriage of subject and form, filling echoing spaces with art and stories much like Zumthor’s architecture does — until eventually, you leave with a new appreciation of the physical world, and your place within it.

schema.headline: ‘From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor’ Review: Wim Wenders’ Latest 3D Documentary Is an Architectural Marvel

title: French President Emmanuel Macron Calls for a ‘New Multilateralism’ Across Creative Industries: ‘We Built a Civilization of Images. We Should Not Resign Ourselves to Watching It Deteriorate’
description: In 1895, the first public film screening happened. It was in the basement of the Grand Café, nearby the Paris Opera, with a program of 10 short movi
body:
In 1895, the first public film screening happened. It was in the basement of the Grand Café, nearby the Paris Opera, with a program of 10 short movies, each no more than 50 seconds long. Cinema was born. The names of the two brothers, Auguste and Louis Lumière, became symbols of an art which needs darkness to make light happens. It heralded a new era of our long-standing Civilization of Images.

	More than a century after, movies and, more broadly, the moving image industry including video games and animation, are more than ever part of our daily lives. From movie theaters, moving images traveled to the television screens and personal devices and, over the past deeply transformative decade, they have found their way into the palms of our hands. One cannot think about visual culture without thinking about screens.
	

	Screens, in themselves, are neutral. They can be an opportunity to get closer to any audience or a source of risk as we all know from the rise of social media and the inflation of images that some have described as a form of cognitive war.


	We see the effects everywhere. Parents worry about their children’s attention. Teachers compete with a permanent flow of images. Artists wonder whether their work can still find an audience. Governments debate technologies that evolve faster than legislation. And each of us knows the strange experience of reaching for a screen for one reason and emerging much later, having forgotten why.

	Yet the screen itself is not our enemy. It has brought extraordinary things into our lives. Never before have so many people had access to so many films, ideas and cultures other than their own. It’s clear to all of us that a screen can educate, connect and inspire.
	

	The question is how to preserve that promise while confronting what has gone wrong. We should begin by acknowledging something uncomfortable: we shaped this world, and we must take responsibility for it. But because we shaped it, we can reshape it. The remedy is not to turn away from screens. It is to change our relationship with them on the screens themselves.

	To remain lucid about the ways our relationship with screens can damage our world, while being ambitious enough to fulfill their promise, we should look to the arts of the moving image: cinema, series and video games. They have been transformed by the digital revolution. But they also show us what a screen can offer at its best: sustained attention, imagination, authorship and a shared experience of another world.

	Here is the paradox. We have never spent so much time in front of screens, and never so little time with the works that these screens were built to carry. Yet those works contain much of what made the moving image so transformative in the first place. A film can send a new generation back to Homer. A series rooted in one language and one place can become a global conversation. A video game can ask us not merely to watch a world, but to inhabit it.

	One distinction therefore matters: the difference between an endless supply of content and works that require time, talent, risk and intention to create.

	The value of these works is economic. If the screen industries lose the capacity to finance ambitious works, take risks on unfamiliar voices or sustain the institutions that bring them to audiences, the consequences will eventually show up on our screens. There may be more images than ever, and fewer genuinely different things to see.

	Their value is also cultural. Works preserve memory, give form to experience and allow one society to enter the imagination of another. They allow cultures to recognize themselves and to discover one another.

	And their value is democratic. A society in which everyone is shown what an algorithm predicts will hold their attention is not quite the same society as one in which citizens still encounter stories, ideas and lives they did not choose in advance. When the systems that shape our attention are optimized above all for engagement, we should not be surprised if public conversation itself becomes shorter, angrier and more fragmented.
	

	The value we give to creative works is therefore not only an economic question for the future of the screen industries. It is a cultural and democratic question for the future of our societies. This is why the moment matters. Several transformations are now happening at once: the fragmentation of attention, the concentration of the channels through which works reach audiences, profound changes in how creation is financed, new forms of production and distribution, and the rapid rise of generative artificial intelligence. Taken separately, each might look like one more disruption an industry will adapt to. Taken together, they are changing the conditions in which images are created, financed, distributed and seen. We should not wait until this new order has become permanent and only then describe it as inevitable.

	Responding requires a method. No single company and no single nation, however large, can find the solution alone.

	What we need is a new form of cooperation: a new multilateralism for the moving image, pursued with the same seriousness we have brought to trade, climate and security. That does not mean building a global bureaucracy for culture. It means bringing to the same table actors who too rarely address these questions together: governments, creators, studios, producers, broadcasters, platforms, cinemas and public institutions.

	Governments do not make films. Artists do not design the technologies through which billions encounter them. Companies cannot define the public interest on their own. And no national institution can respond alone to forces that cross borders by design: technologies, capital, works and audiences.

	The purpose of this dialogue should not be to defend yesterday’s model. It should be to build the conditions for a richer creative future: to preserve the possibility of creating ambitious works, ensure that they can circulate, give audiences the tools to navigate an age of infinite images, and make technological progress compatible with human creativity.

	This conversation must be global.

	That is why, this September, together with the President of the Republic of Korea, I will convene the Lumière Summit. France and South Korea have taken different paths, but both have shown that openness to the world can strengthen, rather than erase, a distinctive creative culture. Governments, artists, companies and institutions will come together to begin building a common response, and to move beyond the divisions of yesterday.
	

	For this moment also offers a rare opportunity for convergence: between cinema, television and gaming; between public authorities and private companies; and between regions of the world that have too often approached these challenges separately. The transformations affecting us are shared. Our response should be as well.

	The United States has shaped an extraordinary part of the history and imagination of the moving image, and its leadership will remain essential to what comes next. Asia has become one of the industry’s greatest creative centers. Across Africa, new generations of storytellers are meeting some of the world’s fastest-growing audiences. The Middle East is home to some of contemporary cinema’s most vital voices. Latin America has repeatedly shown how stories deeply rooted in one place can speak to the world.

	Europe brings its own experience: decades of showing that creative industries can be open to the world without losing their roots, and that economic ambition, technological innovation and cultural sovereignty can strengthen one another.

	France carries a particular responsibility in this conversation. Proud that cinema was born in France 130 years ago, we should not seek to preserve it in amber. Our task is to help create the conditions in which it can be reinvented.

	We built a civilization of images. We should not resign ourselves to watching it deteriorate. The same screens that have become part of the problem can also carry the solution: greater access, greater choice, new forms of creation, new encounters between cultures.

	The task is not to turn back. It is to decide, together, what kind of civilization of images we want to build — and whether we have the ambition to make moving images one of the most valuable Common Goods of our times.

schema.headline: French President Emmanuel Macron Calls for a ‘New Multilateralism’ Across Creative Industries: ‘We Built a Civilization of Images. We Should Not Resign Ourselves to Watching It Deteriorate’

title: Are Russian Filmmakers Finally Coming in From the Cold?
description: The Venice Film Festival found itself under fire in the weeks leading up to opening night over the inclusion of “DAU,” by Russian filmmaker Ilya Khr
body:
The Venice Film Festival found itself under fire in the weeks leading up to opening night over the inclusion of “DAU,” by Russian filmmaker Ilya Khrzhanovsky, in the main competition of its 83rd edition.

	In a joint statement released on Aug. 17, the Ukraine Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Culture and the Ukrainian Embassy in Italy criticized the prestigious fest for selecting what they claimed to be “a project linked to the Russian state and its networks of influence,” maintaining that the decision helped to “restore respectability” to Putin’s pariah state.
	

	The pushback was swift. In an Instagram post responding to the criticism, Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera insisted that “‘DAU’ is not a Russian film; it is not pro-Putin propaganda.” Meanwhile, Khrzhanovsky took to Facebook to refute allegations that the latest installment in his long-running project was backed by Russian financing or is “an instrument of Russian state cultural policy.” 

	Speaking to Variety on the eve of the festival, the director — who renounced his Russian citizenship in 2024 — doubled down, saying: “Since the war started, there was no question of what side I am on, because I am on the side of Ukraine.”

	Coming on the heels of a recent controversy surrounding the Venice Art Biennale’s decision to mount shows by Russian and Israeli artists, the “DAU” dust-up speaks to a larger question hanging over film festivals, cultural institutions and other events that, in the immediate aftermath of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, largely heeded calls for a boycott of Russian cultural exports.
	

	As the war drags deeper into its fifth year, a rapprochement of sorts is underway. While relations with Moscow remain frosty for much of the world, Russian filmmakers are gradually coming in from the cold.

	In the past year alone, Russian-born directors have scooped prizes in Venice (Nastia Korkia’s “Short Summer”) and Cannes (Andrey Zvyagintsev’s “Minotaur”), while Khrzhanovsky is joined on the Lido by fellow exile Victor Kossakovsky, whose latest documentary, “Holly Wood Dust,” premieres out of competition. 

	Though the Oscar-nominated Kossakovsky (“Gunda”) and Khrzhanovsky both left Russia in the 2000s, a broader exodus began not long after Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine in February 2022. Whether fleeing in protest of the Kremlin’s war machine or out of fear of the brutal crackdown on dissent that quickly followed, many of Russian cinema’s most prominent voices left the country, forging exile communities from Tbilisi to Paris, from Berlin to L.A.

	“There are two Russias right now,” says two-time Oscar nominee Alexander Rodnyansky (“Leviathan”), in Venice with Kornél Mundruczó’s “Place to Be,” starring Ellen Burstyn and Taika Waititi. “Russia as the country with this regime controlling everything and censoring all the attempts to speak freely about what’s going on. And there is a Russia outside of the geographical borders.”

	That diaspora is experiencing exile in a variety of ways. The Kyiv-born Rodnyansky, who was sentenced in absentia to 8.5 years in prison by a Moscow court over his opposition to the war, remains determined to support dissenting voices and “make movies with Russian filmmakers, especially young ones, who I feel myself committed to help.” Now based in France, Zvyagintsev likewise remains a trenchant critic of a country he says he has “no intention” of returning to. Though filmed in Latvia, his Cannes Grand Prix-winning “Minotaur” is as scathing a portrait of Russian society under Putin as the director’s previous works.

	For other filmmakers, the westward flight has offered an opportunity for reinvention. Kantemir Balagov’s “Butterfly Jam,” which opened the Directors’ Fortnight section this year in Cannes, stars Barry Keoghan and Riley Keough and is set in an immigrant community in Newark. Director Kirill Sokolov likewise set off for Hollywood; his latest, the blood-soaked revenge farce “They Will Kill You,” stars Zazie Beetz and Patricia Arquette.
	

	Sokolov’s dark comedy “No Looking Back” was among the first films to bear the brunt of the anti-Russia backlash in 2022, when it was pulled from the Glasgow Film Festival over financing that came in part from the Putin regime. The “DAU” controversy in Venice was similarly driven by ties to Russian financiers who would later be sanctioned following the Ukraine invasion.

	But Khrzhanovsky stresses to Variety that their involvement in his decades-spanning project ended years ago; his Venice-bound film is a German production, co-produced with France and Sweden, and has received no Russian funding for seven years, according to the director. 

	As these and other Russian filmmakers set up new lives in exile, the financial ties that once bound them to Putin’s state have been cut. That, as much as their vocal opposition to the Ukraine war, arguably weakens the case for protest and will ease further reentry into the international film community. 

	“They’re shot in Europe. They’re financed in Europe,” says Laurent Danielou, of Paris-based Loco Films, who’s currently financing two features from émigré Russian directors. “They’re not Russian anymore.”

schema.headline: Are Russian Filmmakers Finally Coming in From the Cold?

title: Moonfish’ Director and Stars Lucy Liu and Morgan Spector Break Down Their Black-and-White Animated Film About Isolated Astronauts And Why It’s an Allegory for ‘The Current Human Condition’
description: For Lucy Liu, who has voiced memorable characters in everything from “Kung Fu Panda” to “Strange World,” being part of the independently made, black
body:
For Lucy Liu, who has voiced memorable characters in everything from “Kung Fu Panda” to “Strange World,” being part of the independently made, black-and-white animated film “Moonfish” was all about lending her name and support to first-time filmmaker Daniel Zvereff.

	“These are the people that are not just the creatives, but the ones who are going to be the future,” Liu tells Variety. “I’m just fascinated by how people work and how things start when there’s not all this red tape.”
	

	Premiering at the Venice Film Festival on Sept. 6 after receiving a grant from Biennale College Cinema, “Moonfish” follows a pair of astronauts, voiced by Liu and “The Gilded Age” star Morgan Spector, as they embark on an isolating mission to the moon with a corporate quota to meet if they want to return home.


	“I really wanted to have the film take place in an environment that was an allegory to our current human condition we’re all experiencing right now, where society is very plugged in, but simultaneously we’re all growing a bit disconnected,” Zvereff says.

	Zvereff designed the 2D-animated film so that he could finish it completely on his own, if need be. Thankfully, as Zvereff worked over the course of nine months, he managed to bring on two animators, Hoss Wheeler and Devin Grover.

	“When I watch 2D-animated films, I feel like I’m being exposed to the subconscious of that artist,” Zvereff says of his approach.

	Liu adds, “It’s amazing what digital has done for the speed of animation but you can really feel the appreciation and the craftsmanship [here]. There is a tenderness and an imperfection that I appreciate.”
	

	Unlike Liu, Spector had never done an animated film before “Moonfish.” The trickiest part was getting into his character’s mental headspace as he goes “a little mad,” as Spector puts it.

	“This particular class of people has come to live on the moon, and they’ve evolved, essentially, as moon people. But they’ve also evolved as an underclass; they are the group of people without rights, assets or any real hope for the future,” Spector says of Zvereff’s worldbuilding.

	Liu, of course, also voices the talking fish that accompanies the pair (which Zvereff likens to how miners brought along canaries to know when they had to leave) amidst the mundanity of the corporate tasks at hand.

	“The future that Daniel’s imagining is one in which the relationship between human beings and their tools has been totally inverted. The corporation has merged with the computer in a sort of perfect authoritarian machine that uses human beings as fodder, basically,” Spector says. “It’s a vision of the world that feels continuous with the one we live in.”

	While the film explores isolation and loneliness in space, with the dialogue sparse and to-the-point, Zvereff realized during the writing process that it needed to ultimately be positive about the future of humanity.

	“That’s something that happens as an artist. When you’re making something, you’re taking in all these feelings you’re having and running them through this prism,” he says. “And out comes this beautiful, unexpected light.”

	Watch the trailer: https://youtu.be/Fmsw40R04Bg

body:
California Elderly Woman
                          'Unknown Trouble' Call Leads To Her Arrest For Murder

                              September 6, 2026
                            5:36 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Vicky Kim, an elderly California woman found herself behind bars -- arrested for murder! -- after police responded to a call for "unknown trouble" and then found a person dead, according to authorities.
      
    
            The Riverside County Sheriff's Office said deputies received the cryptic call Friday morning for "unknown trouble" in Palm Desert, California.
      
    
            When the deputies arrived, they discovered a victim suffering from "traumatic injuries consistent with a physical assault,” police said. The victim, who was not identified, was pronounced dead at the scene.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Homicide investigators located 65-year-old Vicky nearby and arrested her in connection with the murder. Kim was booked in the Riverside County jail, where she posed for a smiling mugshot.
      
    
            The sheriff's office did not disclose a motive or details about the alleged crime.

            Andy Williams -- a professional AEW wrestler known as "The Butcher," died Saturday after experiencing a medical emergency during a tag team match in Pennsylvania, according to authorities.
      
    
            The Allegheny County Medical Examiner's Office tells TMZ ... Williams passed away Saturday night following his health crisis at Mr. Small's Theater in Millvale, PA. The Butcher and his partner, The Blade, were battling TME during the Enjoy Wrestling event, leading to its prompt cancellation.  
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A rep for Enjoy Wrestling posted a statement on X, saying that Andy collapsed at the end of his match, and doctors rushed to his aid, giving him CPR before an ambulance arrived to take him to the hospital. The rep also said everyone was sent home, while thanking all the people who gave assistance to Andy. 
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Andy wrestled under the banner of "All-Elite Wrestling" (AEW) with his longtime tag team partner, The Blade. He also played rhythm guitar in a heavy metal band, "Every Time I Die."  
      
    
            Andy was 48.
